subtype: Approach: rebuilding daily routines for sleep and movement [Action]
passage: My brother Lalit stayed with me for a few weeks last spring after a hard year at work, and I watched him build a routine. He chose a sleep time and stuck a note on the bathroom mirror: lights out at eleven. Every evening at seven he walked around the block for twenty minutes, whatever the weather, and after dinner he left his phone in the hall for an hour. He didn't announce a new life. He called it "the small things". I couldn't tell you whether he was happy. Some nights he was quiet at dinner. But by the third week he was up before me, and the walk had become something he did without being asked. He had dropped the idea of changing everything at once. - Kavitha

qa.q: How long was Lalit's evening walk?
What might Lalit have been feeling on the quiet nights at dinner?
qa.a: Kavitha cannot tell for sure, but Lalit might have been tired or low, since the quiet nights sat beside the routine.

qa.q: Why might small routines work better than a big overhaul, and what could Lalit do if he still feels worn out?
qa.a: Small routines are easier to keep up than a sweeping change; if Lalit still feels worn out, he could see a doctor or counsellor.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see the change in Lalit?
qa.a: Kavitha sees steady progress, such as being up early and walking unprompted, while admitting not knowing what Lalit feels inside.

grounding: Lalit sets a regular sleep time, a twenty-minute evening walk and a screen-free hour, small routines rather than an overhaul.
